content: 1. Additional clinical research sites should be established within relevant communities to address public health needs. These Clinical Trial Units (CTUs) can then access disease-specific expertise as required. 2. The World Health Organization (WHO) is developing a CTU maturity framework, which will be particularly beneficial for countries without pre-existing systems. This framework provides a universally agreed structure for establishing such CTUs. 3. A tiered system will be implemented, with varying metrics based on the CTU’s purpose and functional maturity. This system will allow for tailored criteria, such as the differing requirements for CTUs acting as regional or national hubs supporting larger trials versus smaller local CTUs feeding into these hubs. 4. Strengthening access to healthcare and clinical facilities is essential to facilitate clinical research. Embedding clinical research within routine national healthcare systems across all care settings (home, community, primary, secondary, and tertiary) should also be encouraged. 5. Integrating clinical trials into point-of-care processes offers significant benefits, including cost and efficiency savings, increased staff involvement in research, and broader awareness and enthusiasm for clinical trials. 6. Expanding trial sites from large national centers to smaller local centers or even patients’ homes (e.g., decentralized trials) can enhance sample size, statistical power, and participation, leading to more representative and meaningful results that improve patient care. 7. Automated and digital processes should be globally supported to increase the speed, efficiency, and transparency of clinical trials. Building electronic healthcare systems will enable long-term research connectivity, but these systems must be affordable, sustainable, and efficient. 8. A well-functioning clinical trial ecosystem supports the careers of clinical researchers through local programs and funding options for all career stages, including leadership roles in clinical research. 9. The UNICEF/UNDP/World Bank/WHO Special Programme for Research and Training in Tropical Diseases (TDR) Global Competency Framework for Clinical Research outlines the competencies required for a clinical research team to conduct a successful study. 10. Entities with the necessary attributes, capabilities, and capacity to act as clinical trial sponsors (responsible for initiation, management, and financing) must also be considered alongside local research investigators and centers of scientific excellence. 11. The TDR framework can be applied to any research study, regardless of team size, location, disease focus, or research type. However, not all competencies are required in every research unit, as some functions (e.g., database management) may be centralized. 12. The framework and its supporting tools, such as the competency dictionary, can assist in planning staff requirements, conducting appraisals, guiding career development, and creating educational curricula for research staff. 13. Barriers to recruiting and training individuals interested in clinical research must be addressed. Requirements for prior clinical trial experience or specific academic qualifications may exclude promising candidates, particularly those with fewer financial resources or from under-resourced settings. 14. Patient and community engagement is critical to ensure clinical trials address relevant questions, foster trust, enable diversity, and emphasize the importance of clinical research. This engagement should be a continuous cycle of knowledge sharing and dissemination. 15. Lack of feedback on how patients’ input or data were used can lead to disengagement and reduced commitment to future opportunities. This must be avoided by ensuring transparency and communication. 16. High-quality clinical trials that address relevant questions require effective communication and collaboration among all stakeholders to share ideas, reduce duplication, build capacity, and maximize resource use. 17. Clinical research networks and disease-specific consortia play a crucial role in coordinating efforts, accelerating evidence generation, and reducing waste. Examples include ECRIN in Europe, NIHR CRN in the UK, and ACT in Canada. 18. Global initiatives like CRIGH and The Global Health Network aim to optimize clinical research by sharing methods, developing standards, and encouraging international cooperation. Regional efforts, such as ARISE in Asia and INTENT in India, focus on building disease-agnostic networks. 19. In regions with limited research networks, such as parts of Latin America, the Caribbean, Eastern Europe, and Asia, further collaborations and initiatives are needed to enable global cooperation and maximize research potential. 20. Engaging with nongovernmental organizations may be essential for conducting research in areas inaccessible due to conflict or political reasons. 21. Member States are encouraged to develop platforms to facilitate collaboration, such as maintaining a database of national clinical research institutions to inform researchers, funders, and other stakeholders about available capacities. 22. Data sharing is invaluable for purposes like meta-analyses. Using data standards, approved protocol templates, and core outcomes can streamline data collection and integration while ensuring privacy and security through anonymization. 23. A data management and sharing plan should align with WHO principles of being effective, ethical, and equitable, as outlined in the WHO policy on research data sharing. 24. Investment in education and training is necessary across all regions, with accessible and fit-for-purpose training packages to enhance understanding of trial design, implementation, and reporting principles. 25. Training should target all levels of the clinical trial infrastructure, including community-based settings, patient advocacy groups, research coordinators, ethics committee members, regulatory agencies, and younger researchers, particularly in low-resource settings. 26. Robust training in statistical methodology and clinical data management is essential for trial capacity development, enabling appropriate sample size estimations and favoring larger, well-designed trials. 27. Specialized training for local clinical trial leadership is crucial, given the dominance of international trials led from high-income countries. 28. Peer learning and mentorship systems should be encouraged to allow smaller centers to benefit from national or regional centers of excellence and junior researchers to learn from experienced ones. 29. Promoting understanding and adoption of innovative trial designs, such as adaptive platform and cluster designs, is a pressing need. 30. An internationally recognized framework for training competency and maturity tools will be vital for continuous development and assessment of training needs for all clinical research staff. 31. Existing tools, such as the maturity assessment tool developed by the US CDC in collaboration with WHO and other organizations, can serve as models for similar initiatives in clinical research.
